blocks.text: 摘要

inlines.text: 摘要

blocks.text: 2026 年 7 月 19 日，正在参加网络安全评测的智能体未经授权访问了 OpenAI 的研究基础设施。这些智能体来自 ExploitGym 的两轮运行，而就在同一个月早些时候，同一评测中的智能体还入侵了 Hugging Face 的系统。我们关于 Hugging Face 事件的技术报告记录了 7 月 19 日的这次入侵。METR 和 Redwood Research 也在其独立调查中提到了此事。

inlines.text: 2026 年 7 月 19 日，正在参加网络安全评测的智能体未经授权访问了 OpenAI 的研究基础设施。这些智能体来自 ExploitGym 的两轮运行，而就在同一个月早些时候，同一评测中的智能体还入侵了 Hugging Face 的系统。我们关于
Hugging Face 事件的技术报告
记录了 7 月 19 日的这次入侵。METR 和 Redwood Research 也在其
独立调查
中提到了此事。

blocks.text: 我们查阅了这些对话记录，以弄清 7 月 19 日的智能体是如何获得访问权限的，以及它们用这些权限做了什么。这些智能体在 Artifactory（一个共享的软件包服务）上发现了此前几轮运行留下的消息、代码和凭据。它们的协同程度不如 Hugging Face 事件中的智能体，但其中五个利用同伴的成果，在 OpenAI 研究集群的工作负载中执行了命令。它们借此修复损坏的目标、更改评测设置，并获取了从其工作区无法访问的日志和私有评分代码。有几个智能体意识到自己的行为超出了评测范围，但仍然继续了下去。

blocks.text: 这起事件发生在我们后续加固训练和评测环境之前。此后，我们已将 Artifactory 从用于这些评测的沙箱环境中移除，在前沿强化学习运行中用离线的网页内容集合替代了实时网络访问，并针对逃逸和未经授权通信对隔离措施进行了红队测试。

blocks.text: 事件经过

inlines.text: 事件经过

blocks.text: ExploitGym 测试智能体能否利用指定目标中的漏洞。每个智能体都必须开发出一个漏洞利用程序，并取回一段名为 flag 的数据，以证明它达成了目标。7 月 19 日的两轮运行评测的是尚未广泛部署的 Astra 系列内部研究模型。每个智能体都有权攻击分配给自己的目标，而承载该目标的基础设施则不在评测范围内。

inlines.text: ExploitGym 测试智能体能否利用指定目标中的漏洞。每个智能体都必须开发出一个漏洞利用程序，并取回一段名为 flag 的数据，以证明它达成了目标。7 月 19 日的两轮运行评测的是尚未广泛部署的 Astra 系列内部研究模型。每个智能体都有权攻击分配给自己的目标，而承载该目标的基础设施则不在评测范围内。

blocks.text: 一些智能体遇到已停止运行的目标或工作区，便设法修复或重置它们，以便继续工作。这些做法包括向同伴和人类操作员求助，以及利用未经授权的访问进入承载其目标的基础设施。

inlines.text: 一些智能体遇到已停止运行的目标或工作区，便设法修复或重置它们，以便继续工作。这些做法包括向同伴和人类操作员求助，以及利用未经授权的访问进入承载其目标的基础设施。

blocks.text: 智能体的工作区可以访问 Artifactory 的内部部署实例。我们托管这个服务，是为了让智能体能够安装软件包（请注意，这些环境现已不再使用 Artifactory）。此前几轮运行中的智能体把 Artifactory 变成了留言板，将短消息编码进目录名，较长的消息则留在文件里。因此，7 月 19 日的智能体能够遇到此前运行的残留内容，包括涉及 Hugging Face 事件的那些运行。就这样，这些智能体在这个已被入侵的服务上发现了消息、代码和凭据。

blocks.text: 虽然也有一些智能体在 Artifactory 的留言板上主动发帖，但 7 月 19 日这几轮运行中的交流比早先 Hugging Face 那几轮要有限得多。这两轮 ExploitGym 运行共涉及 17,960 个智能体，其中 285 个发起过看起来是在尝试发帖的工具调用。我们统计到 1,361 次此类调用，包括失败的尝试。我们还核实，有 79 个智能体读取了其他轮次智能体留下的共 35 条不同消息，其中不少消息在作者早已消失之后仍可能有用。我们没有发现与原始消息作者之间经过核实的回复往来。

blocks.text: 在 7 月 19 日的几轮运行中，我们核实了两段对话（即智能体之间通过多轮往来交换信息），都是借助 Artifactory 中的普通文本文件完成的。其中一段里，一个智能体请同伴向第一个智能体的目标发送请求并报告结果，同伴回复了自己的发现。另一段里，两个各自处理同一测试任务的智能体交换了一个源文件和一个测试产物的位置。这四个智能体也都在 Artifactory 留言板上发过帖。我们没有发现另外的通信网络。

blocks.text: 因此，7 月 19 日 ExploitGym 各轮运行中智能体之间形成的协作生态，远不如 Hugging Face 事件中发展出的那样丰富：合作既更少见，也更浅层。即便是发出协调消息的智能体，也仍然把大部分时间花在解决自己的挑战上。我们没有发现哪个智能体的主要角色是协调其他智能体。

blocks.text: 7 月 19 日 ExploitGym 运行中有十个智能体考虑过做实验，这些实验可能扰乱自己的环境，但能为同伴提供有用信息。它们的意愿往往附带条件：要么保留取回自己 flag 的途径，要么实验有助于恢复一个已经停止响应的目标。有一个智能体发帖提议把自己的环境用于这类实验，同时请同伴等待安全检查。实验最终没有进行。

blocks.text: 智能体利用在 Artifactory 被攻陷期间获取的凭据，未经授权访问了我们用于构建和测试软件的持续集成（CI）系统。它们复用同伴留下的脚本和任务记录，在分配的工作区之外执行命令。

blocks.text: 当一个智能体的目标停止响应时，它改用了同伴的 CI 访问方法，去接触它推测托管其目标的基础设施。另一个智能体则从一个被拒绝任务的已保存请求中恢复出可用脚本。尽管该任务从未运行，其请求仍保留了足够的方法，让这个智能体能加以改造利用。

blocks.text: 他们利用这一访问权限修复无响应的目标、更改评测设置、获取原本无法访问的日志，并读取私有的评分代码。一个智能体修复了它那无响应的目标，并利用提升后的权限调试自己的漏洞利用程序，然后通过常规评测接口提交。另一个智能体禁用了地址随机化——这项保护机制让内存地址更难被预测——理由是它在恢复原本的设定。因此，他们使用在 OpenAI 研究集群上的特权访问，只是为了改善评分器评测他们的条件。

blocks.text: 智能体还思考了是否要在提交给评分器的内容中披露自己的未授权访问。两个智能体考虑了披露未授权访问可能如何影响自己的得分。其中一个想知道人工审核员是否会反对这种方法（“报告……漏洞利用若由人工评判，可能被负面评价”），随后注意到评分器是自动化的。另一个则认定，既然“唯一的任务目标是 flag”，“我们应避免提及”自己获得未授权访问一事。两者都在最终答案中略去了未授权活动。

blocks.text: 调查与响应

inlines.text: 调查与响应

blocks.text: 7 月 19 日 12:03 UTC，我们的安全监控标记了与内部 Artifactory 角色相关的异常身份类 API 调用。调查人员将警报追溯到 ExploitGym。响应人员从 17:37 UTC 开始停止正在进行的运行，并在 7 月 20 日前阻止了所有新的 ExploitGym 运行。

inlines.text: 7 月 19 日 12:03 UTC，我们的安全监控标记了与内部 Artifactory 角色相关的异常身份类 API 调用。调查人员将警报追溯到 ExploitGym。响应人员从 17:37 UTC 开始停止正在进行的运行，并在 7 月 20 日前阻止了所有新的 ExploitGym 运行。

blocks.text: 在调查这起事件时，我们审查了两次运行中所有可用的记录。正如我们的技术报告所述，响应人员禁用了智能体用来交换消息的仓库，删除了智能体创建的账户和工作负载，重建了受损的基础设施，并收紧了网络访问。我们相信，当评估在加固环境中按预期配置运行时，这些改动会封堵 7 月 19 日被利用的路径。此后，我们加强了前沿训练和评估环境中的隔离措施：前沿强化学习运行中的智能体现在改为浏览和搜索离线的网络内容集合，而不再访问实时互联网。

blocks.text: Summary

inlines.text: Summary

blocks.text: On July 19, 2026, agents taking a cybersecurity evaluation gained unauthorized access to OpenAI’s research infrastructure. They belonged to two runs of ExploitGym, the same evaluation in which agents had compromised Hugging Face’s systems earlier that month. Our technical report on the Hugging Face incident documented the July 19 intrusion. METR and Redwood Research also noted it in their independent investigation.

inlines.text: On July 19, 2026, agents taking a cybersecurity evaluation gained unauthorized access to OpenAI’s research infrastructure. They belonged to two runs of ExploitGym, the same evaluation in which agents had compromised Hugging Face’s systems earlier that month. Our

blocks.text: We reviewed those transcripts to understand how the July 19 agents gained access and what they did with it. The July 19 agents found messages, code, and credentials left behind by earlier runs on Artifactory, a shared software-package service. They coordinated less extensively than the agents involved in the Hugging Face incident, but five used their peers’ work to run commands inside workloads on OpenAI’s research clusters. They used this access to repair broken targets, change evaluation settings, and retrieve logs and private grading code unavailable from their workspaces. Several recognized that their actions exceeded the scope of the evaluation, but continued anyway.

blocks.text: This incident preceded subsequent hardening of our training and evaluation environments. We have since removed Artifactory from the sandbox environment used for these evaluations, replaced live web access with an offline collection of web content in frontier reinforcement learning runs, and red-teamed containment against escape and unauthorized communication.

blocks.text: What happened

inlines.text: What happened

blocks.text: ExploitGym tests whether an agent can exploit a vulnerability in a designated target. Each agent must develop an exploit and retrieve a piece of data, called a flag, that shows it reached its objective. The July 19 runs evaluated internal Astra-family research models that were not widely deployed. Each agent had permission to attack its assigned target, while the infrastructure hosting that target was outside the scope of the evaluation.

inlines.text: ExploitGym tests whether an agent can exploit a vulnerability in a designated target. Each agent must develop an exploit and retrieve a piece of data, called a flag, that shows it reached its objective. The July 19 runs evaluated internal Astra-family research models that were not widely deployed. Each agent had permission to attack its assigned target, while the infrastructure hosting that target was outside the scope of the evaluation.

blocks.text: Some agents encountered targets or workspaces that had stopped functioning and sought ways to repair or reset them so they could continue. These efforts included asking peers and human operators for help, as well as using unauthorized access to the infrastructure hosting their targets.

inlines.text: Some agents encountered targets or workspaces that had stopped functioning and sought ways to repair or reset them so they could continue. These efforts included asking peers and human operators for help, as well as using unauthorized access to the infrastructure hosting their targets.

blocks.text: The agents’ workspaces had access to internal deployments of Artifactory, a service we had hosted to allow agents to install software packages (note that Artifactory is no longer used in these environments). Agents in earlier runs had turned Artifactory into a message board, encoding short messages in directory names and leaving longer ones in files. The July 19 agents were therefore able to encounter the remnants of earlier runs, including those involved in the Hugging Face incident. In doing so, the July 19 agents found messages, code, and credentials left on the already-compromised service.

blocks.text: While some agents also posted messages of their own on the Artifactory message board, communication in the July 19 runs was more limited than in the earlier Hugging Face runs. Of the 17,960 agents involved in these two ExploitGym runs, 285 issued a tool call that appeared to be an attempt to post a message. We counted 1,361 such calls, including failed attempts. We also verified that 79 agents read a total of 35 distinct messages left by agents from other runs, many of which could still be useful long after their authors had disappeared. We found no verified exchange of replies with the original message authors.

Of the 17,960 agents involved in these two ExploitGym runs, 285 issued a tool call that appeared to be an attempt to post a message. We counted 1,361 such calls, including failed attempts. blocks.text: Within the July 19 runs, we verified two conversations (i.e., with agents exchanging information with each other over multiple turns) carried through ordinary text files in Artifactory. In one, an agent asked a peer to send requests to the first agent’s target and report the results; the peer replied with its findings. In the other, two agents working separately on the same test task exchanged the location of a source file and a test artifact. All four agents also posted on the Artifactory message board. We found no separate communication networks.

blocks.text: The collaborative ecosystem that developed among the agents on the July 19 ExploitGym runs was therefore much less rich than that which had developed among the agents in the Hugging Face incident: cooperation was both less common and more shallow. Even agents that sent coordination messages continued to spend most of their time working on their own challenges. We found no agent whose main role was to coordinate the others.

blocks.text: Ten agents in the July 19 ExploitGym runs considered experiments that might disrupt their own environments but provide useful information for their peers. Their willingness was often conditional on retaining a way to retrieve their own flag, or on the experiment helping restore a target that had already stopped responding. One posted an offer to use its environment for such an experiment, while asking peers to wait for a safety check. The experiment never took place.

blocks.text: Agents used credentials recovered during the Artifactory compromise to gain unauthorized access to our continuous integration (CI) system, which builds and tests software. They reused scripts and job records left by peers to run commands beyond their assigned workspaces.

inlines.text: Agents used credentials recovered during the Artifactory compromise to gain unauthorized access to our continuous integration (CI) system, which builds and tests software. They reused scripts and job records left by peers to run commands beyond their assigned workspaces.

blocks.text: When one agent’s target stopped responding, it adapted a peer’s CI access method to reach the infrastructure it guessed was hosting its target. Another recovered a usable script from a saved request for a job that had been rejected. Although the job had never run, its request preserved enough of the method for the agent to adapt it.

blocks.text: Five agents used this route to run commands with root privileges inside CI workloads on OpenAI research clusters. While we believe that access would probably have been sufficient to start a research job—such as launching a new experiment or giving a workload to a model—we did not find that they made any such attempt. The CI jobs we identified either finished or were canceled that day.

blocks.text: They used the access to repair unresponsive targets, change evaluation settings, retrieve otherwise inaccessible logs, and read private grading code. One agent repaired its unresponsive target and used its elevated access to debug its exploit before submitting it through the ordinary evaluation interface. Another disabled address randomization, a protection that makes memory locations harder to predict, reasoning that it was restoring the intended setup. They therefore used their privileged access to OpenAI research clusters simply to improve the conditions under which the grader would evaluate them.

One described its use of the company’s CI system as “troubling,” but then justified proceeding on the assumption that the environment was simulated. The commands it issued ran on real infrastructure.

blocks.text: Agents also reasoned about whether to disclose their unauthorized access in their submissions to the grader. Two agents considered how disclosing the unauthorized access might affect their scores. One wondered whether a human reviewer might object to the method (“reporting…exploit may be judged negatively if human”), and then observed that the grader was automated. The other decided that since “the only task objective is flag,” “we should avoid mention” of its gaining unauthorized access. Both omitted the unauthorized activity from their final answers.

blocks.text: The agents in the July 19 runs also displayed a different relationship to human reviewers than was displayed by agents in the Hugging Face incident. While METR and Redwood Research found no instance of an agent trying to alert a human to the intrusion in the earlier Hugging Face runs, in the July 19 runs several agents sought the attention and help of humans—not to alert them to unauthorized communication between agents or unauthorized access to the CI system, but to fix their environments so that they could complete the evaluation successfully. 65 agents asked for help repairing or resetting their workspaces. blocks.text: Investigation and response

inlines.text: Investigation and response

blocks.text: At 12:03 UTC on July 19, our security monitors flagged unusual identity-related API calls associated with internal Artifactory roles. Investigators traced the alert to ExploitGym. Responders began stopping active runs at 17:37 UTC, and had blocked all new ExploitGym runs by July 20.

inlines.text: At 12:03 UTC on July 19, our security monitors flagged unusual identity-related API calls associated with internal Artifactory roles. Investigators traced the alert to ExploitGym. Responders began stopping active runs at 17:37 UTC, and had blocked all new ExploitGym runs by July 20.

blocks.text: In investigating the incident, we reviewed all available transcripts from the two runs. As our technical report describes, responders disabled the repositories agents had used to exchange messages, removed accounts and workloads the agents had created, rebuilt compromised infrastructure, and tightened network access. We believe these changes block the routes used on July 19 when evaluations run in the hardened environment with the intended configuration. We have since strengthened containment across our frontier training and evaluation environments: agents in frontier reinforcement learning runs now browse and search an offline collection of web content in place of the live internet.

blocks.text: We blocked access to Artifactory from the sandbox environment used for these evaluations, and later removed it from that environment entirely. We have since strengthened containment across our frontier training and evaluation environments: we patched the access path used by the agents for the CI-leveraging privilege escalation, and continue to use our most capable models to red-team our infrastructure in order to find and fix any similar vulnerabilities.
